synopsis: This accepted September 30 preprint contributes an author-run controlled comparison of autonomous ML engineering systems. For pieces 01–03, it supplies evidence about delegating pipeline exploration to a single coding-agent session, judging results through validation-based selection and matched comparisons, and accounting for inference and hardware costs. Its evidentiary role is reported experimental evidence supporting a simple baseline under the tested conditions, not independent replication or proof that orchestration never helps. The authors report a GLM 5.2 medal-rate advantage for Malena, while weaker-model results and evaluation qualifications constrain generalization. These orientation statements do not replace passage citations.
limitations_and_counterevidence: The authors evaluate their own system and acknowledge possible tuning asymmetry, contamination, limited statistical power and restricted coordination experiments. Gemma significantly favors MLEvolve on percentile; the source's wording about an equivalent medal rate must not be treated as an equivalence test. Main ablations and external comparisons use different task preparations, with additional subset exceptions elsewhere in the text. NatureBench permits repeated evaluation queries and reports oracle best-of-run scores, so it does not provide an untouched final-test confirmation. Minimal architecture is not necessarily cheaper: the reported inference costs are modeled, and backbone hosting is separate from worker hardware. Implementation descriptions and repair diffs support inspectability, but the supplied material provides no independent replication. All later substantive claims require the exact passages below or additional validated extractions.

passages.purpose: Methods and trustworthiness: defines self-selection versus oracle selection, fixed-task confidence intervals, framework version and experiment-worker resources (§3).

locator.quote:
We build our harness on the OpenCode v1.15.6 coding agent framework ([OpenCode Contributors, 2026](#bib.bib33)), and our primary benchmark is MLE-bench ([Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)), with task selection described in Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1).
When reporting performance of a method that produces several submissions, we distinguish between self-selection, where the reported submission is the one with the best validation score reported by the agent, and oracle selection, where it is the one with the best hidden test score.
Unless otherwise specified, we report self-selected performance. Percentile indicates the percentage of human leaderboard entries that score worse than the agent.
We report 95% Confidence Intervals (CIs) on macro-task averages, holding the set of tasks fixed and bootstrapping on the seeds available for each task.
Unless otherwise stated, we report results with the GLM 5.2 backbone; Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4) lists all models used.
Across all experiments, agents’ resources stay fixed at 1\(\times\)A100 80GB, 12 CPU cores and 144GB of RAM; backbones are served locally with vLLM ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)).

passages.purpose: Delegation procedure: specifies what the single-session agent controls and the harness's continuation mechanism (§4.3).

locator.quote:
The Malena iteration is also built on the coding agent infrastructure but, instead of being prompted to produce a single submission, runs a single session spanning the entire time budget, only briefly prompted to continue working whenever a turn ends.
This lets the agent drive exploration, exploitation and its own knowledge base autonomously.

passages.purpose: Reported headline comparison: matched model, hardware and budget; GLM 5.2 medal rates and the authors' statistical qualification (§6). Attribute these findings to the study.

locator.quote: Holding the model, hardware, and budget fixed, none of the published harnesses we tested significantly outperforms the plain agent session with frontier backbones. With GLM 5.2, Malena earns a medal on 62.5% of the competitions, compared with 47.1% for the best external harness tested. Across all backbones, our statistical analysis either favours Malena over the other harnesses or finds no significant medal-rate difference between them.

passages.purpose: Counterevidence and backbone dependence: preserves the significant Gemma percentile regression and mixed results across metrics (D.2). The authors' 'equivalent' wording does not establish statistical equivalence.

locator.quote:
We find that Malena outperforms every presented baseline at the GLM 5.2 backbone across both performance metrics; obtains strictly better percentile scores for Kimi K3, and either beats or comes up as statistically indistinguishable at the DeepSeek V4 Flash.
The only backbone where Malena presents a significant regression against other baselines is with Gemma 4 31B — the weaker of all models tested — where MLEvolve outperforms according to the percentile metric, while maintaining an equivalent medal rate at our current statistical power.

passages.purpose: Evaluation integrity and reproducibility: distinguishes original default29 ablations from repaired fixed30 external comparisons and identifies leakage or missing-data concerns (A.1).

locator.quote:
Results presented in Section [4](#S4) are reported on the original MLE-bench without any intervention, and in the 29 task split (without either bms or alaska2).
This split is referred to in this work as the default29 task split.
We note that a subset of our tasks has been previously reported containing issues in the MLE-bench preparation scripts.
Such issues may include missing data needed to correctly train ML pipelines, data present that leaks the ground truth predictions, etc.
We have identified four competitions that could either lead to impossible tasks or are susceptible to cheating.
In order to maintain a fair comparison set between our baselines and other tested public harnesses, we fixed such issues and report their performance for all results in this paper when comparing against existing baselines.
Such tasks are marked with ‡ in Table [3](#A1.T3) and the split is labeled as the fixed30 set in this paper.
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2) lists the exact code diffs applied to the MLE-bench preparation scripts, together with the underlying bugs they address.

passages.purpose: Qualification of scientific-task evaluation: preserves unlimited online scoring, oracle selection, success threshold and eight-hour budget (A.3). This protocol cannot support a claim of untouched-test confirmation.

locator.quote:
NatureBench ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib43)) asks an agent to try to match or
exceed the published state-of-the-art result of a recent Nature-family paper on
that paper’s own held-out evaluation protocol. Unlike fixed30’s Kaggle
competitions, there is no external leaderboard to compute a percentile against: each task
ships a dedicated evaluation service that the agent may query online, unlimited times,
via an /evaluate endpoint that returns the candidate’s score. We follow
NatureBench’s own protocol and report a task as surpassed when its normalized gain score
\(g>0.1\). We report the beat-SOTA rate — the
fraction of tasks on which the best score achieved anywhere in the run (oracle) surpasses
the published SOTA — macro-averaged over a licensed task cohort at an 8h time budget, for both a GLM 5.2 and a Kimi K3 backbone.

passages.purpose: Cost counterevidence: the simpler agent has higher modeled GLM 5.2 inference cost; preserves the cache-accounting explanation (§5.1). These are not measured total deployment bills.

locator.quote:
Although total token volumes are comparable across agentic harnesses, cost is driven
almost entirely by cache-read tokens. At GLM 5.2, Malena’s modeled
USD cost ($12.12) is \(\approx\)6.2\(\times\) AiScientist’s ($1.95), even though its input and
output token volumes are comparable to Arbor’s and AiScientist’s --- only its cache-read
usage is roughly an order of magnitude higher. This follows directly from Malena running as a single ever-growing session that resends its whole prior context every turn
(the same-session cache model still prices that resent context, even though it credits
most of it as a cache hit); Arbor and AiScientist instead reset into fresh, shorter-lived
threads per branch or submission, so their modeled cache-read volume never grows as large.

passages.purpose: Cost and replication requirements: separates eight-GPU backbone hosting from worker resources and documents price assumptions and missing real cache-hit telemetry (A.4).

locator.quote:
All backbones are served locally with vLLM ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)) on 8\(\times\)B200 or 8\(\times\)A100 80GB nodes for smaller models.
Unless otherwise specified, all models run with reasoning enabled at their maximum available configuration, and at their canonical maximum sequence length.
Input and output costs, when reported, are the weighted effective per-token prices listed
for each backbone on [https://openrouter.ai/](https://openrouter.ai/) — a marketplace that aggregates
multiple inference providers per model and reports a usage-weighted effective price across
them, rather than any single provider’s list price — snapshotted around September 2026.
Cache-read cost is modeled as \(0.1\times\) the input cost: none of the harnesses compared
here report real cache-hit token counts directly (see the per-method telemetry notes in
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1) and Appendix [D.4](#A4.SS4)), so this
is a fixed discount applied uniformly rather than a per-backbone reported cache price.

passages.purpose: Author-acknowledged limitations: contamination, statistical uncertainty, coordination scope and possible tuning asymmetry. Preserve the authors' confidence in weaker claims as their interpretation, not established equivalence.

locator.quote:
Most of our results rely on MLE-bench, which has known task-preparation
issues and, being built from public Kaggle competitions, is a plausible contamination target;
we mitigate this by fixing broken tasks, directly checking for contamination, and additionally
evaluating on NatureBench. A second limitation is statistical power: some results still have
confidence intervals wide enough to preclude strong claims about effect size, though we believe
the weaker no-worse-than claims are well supported.
A third is scope: most harness interventions we test operate within a single worker, and we leave a more in-depth exploration of sophisticated inter-agent coordination protocols to future work.
A fourth is possible asymmetry in tuning effort between Malena and the external harnesses it is compared against; Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3) documents the backbone-specific bug fixes and configuration ablations we applied to each external harness to mitigate this.

passages.purpose: Reproducibility contribution and boundary: identifies documented settings, models, task lists, repair diffs and statistical methods. This documentation statement does not establish released complete run artifacts or independent replication.

locator.quote:
Full experimental settings are described in Section [3](#S3) and in
Appendix [B](#A2): the coding agent framework and tool set exposed to the
model in each iteration (Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2)), the search strategies compared
(Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3)), and the exact LLM backbones and hosting configuration
used, with their HuggingFace identifiers (Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4)). The task sets used for
both benchmarks are listed in full in Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1) (MLE-bench, including which
tasks we fixed to remove data or ground-truth-leakage issues, and why) and
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3) (NatureBench); the exact code diffs we applied to fix the
affected MLE-bench preparation scripts are given in Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2). Our
statistical methodology — how macro-task averages, bootstrap confidence intervals, and
paired-by-task comparisons are computed — is described in Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5).
